Sarah and Hagar
SAIR-uh and HAY-gar
proper nouns (Old Testament figures)
Sarah (Hebrew Sarah) means "princess," the freeborn wife of Abraham; Hagar (Hebrew Hagar) was her Egyptian bondwoman, whose name is linked to wandering or flight.

📖 Biblical Definition

Sarah the freewoman and Hagar the bondwoman stand together in the history of Genesis 16 and 21 as the two mothers of Abraham's house, and the apostle Paul declares them an allegory of the two covenants. When the promised seed delayed, Sarah gave her Egyptian handmaid to Abraham, and Hagar conceived Ishmael after the flesh by the strength of nature and the impatience of unbelief. But the LORD had promised a son by Sarah, and in due time Isaac was born after the Spirit, the child of promise, when both parents were as good as dead. The mocking of the bondwoman's son against the heir of promise brought the casting out of Hagar and Ishmael, which Paul in Galatians 4 sets forth as a type: Hagar answers to Mount Sinai, the covenant of bondage and works, gendering to bondage with her children; Sarah answers to the Jerusalem which is above, the mother of the free, the covenant of grace whose children are born by promise. So the believer learns he is not a child of the bondwoman but of the free, justified not by the works of the law but by faith in the promised Seed. Yet the LORD heard the cry of the lad and showed mercy even to Hagar in the wilderness, for He is gracious.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Abraham's wife and her Egyptian bondwoman, whom the apostle expounds as a figure of the two covenants of bondage and of grace.

SARAH AND HAGAR, proper nouns. Sarah, "princess," the freewoman; Hagar, the Egyptian bondwoman of Abraham's household.

The two mothers whose sons, Isaac and Ishmael, divide the line of the flesh from the line of promise.

In Paul's allegory, a figure of Sinai in bondage and of the heavenly Jerusalem in freedom (Gal 4).

As it is written, "Cast out the bondwoman and her son: for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman" (Gen 21:10).

A type teaching justification by promise and faith, not by the works of the law.

📖 Key Scripture

Gen 16:15 — "And Hagar bare Abram a son: and Abram called his son's name, which Hagar bare, Ishmael."

Gen 21:2 — "For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him."

Gen 21:10 — "Wherefore she said unto Abraham, Cast out this bondwoman and her son: for the son of this bondwoman shall not be heir with my son, even with Isaac."

Gal 4:31 — "So then, brethren, we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Modern readings sometimes recast Sarah as oppressor and Hagar merely as victim, eclipsing the covenantal typology the apostle himself draws.

expand to see more

Where the Spirit through Paul gives us an allegory of bondage and freedom, of law and grace, contemporary retellings often flatten the account into a story of social grievance, casting Hagar simply as the wronged outsider and Sarah as the privileged abuser. This inverts the inspired interpretation. Genesis does record Sarah's harshness and Hagar's affliction without excusing them, and it shows the tender mercy of the LORD who hears the bondwoman's cry; but the canonical point is not a parable of victimhood.

The principle to recover is the apostolic typology itself. Hagar and Sinai gender to bondage; the works of the law cannot bring forth the heir. Sarah and the Jerusalem above gender to freedom; the child of promise is born by grace through faith. To read the narrative aright is to find in it the very gospel of justification, and to rejoice that we are children not of the bondwoman but of the free.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The account is rooted in the promise of a seed to Abraham and its fulfillment against the impatience of the flesh.

expand to see more

The covenant of Genesis 15 promised Abraham a son from his own body.

Hagar's son Ishmael was conceived by human contrivance when faith faltered (Gen 16).

Isaac, the child of promise, was born at the set time God had appointed (Gen 21:2).

Paul interprets the two women as the two covenants in Galatians 4:22-31.

The casting out of the bondwoman prefigures that law and grace cannot share the inheritance.

Usage

""The bondwoman and the freewoman" is shorthand for the contrast of law and gospel."

"Isaac as "the child of promise" names every believer born again by grace."

"Hagar's well, Beer-lahai-roi, marks the place where God who sees showed mercy to the afflicted."
